The View from SomewherePart IV · Inference at the edge

Chapter 16

Three repairs and their price

Web edition. Figure 16.3 is live: you can change the sample size and the slack, probe a point, and rerun the toy’s four rules.

Chapter 15 explains one number, and I want you to keep it in front of you. Take a population that is perfectly coherent, one whose three survey tables glue, but built so that an upward drift in one survey has used up every bit of slack the cut rule allows. Draw samples from it and ask whether the estimated shortfall C^ is positive. It is, in 14 to 21 percent of the samples, at sample sizes from 1,000 to 64,000 per survey. The rate does not shrink as the samples grow. The rule “declare incoherence when C^>0” is a test with a nominal level of 5 percent and an actual level of three to four times that, and more data does not help.

This chapter is about three ways of getting the level back, and about what each one costs. I will say the verdict first, so that you can read the rest as evidence. In the cells we tried, all three procedures held the level, with one qualification for the third. They differ in what they ask you to believe and in how often they catch a real contradiction. The first has a proof that reduces to a published theorem, and little power at moderate sample sizes. The second has more power and no proof at all. The third has a theorem behind it, with conditions we did not check, and it has a tuning parameter that trades the false alarms against the power.

16.1What we carry in

A reminder of the objects, in the form this chapter needs them. Three surveys report tables on ordered answers. C≥0 is the shortfall of the cut rule: over all joint distributions of the six survey-specific copies that reproduce the tables, the least value of the smaller of the two crossing probabilities at each cut, summed over cuts and variables. The null is C=0. D and W are the other two quantities of Chapter 14: D is the optimal value of a linear program whose right-hand side is the tables, W is the transport gap between the shared margins, and D=W+2C. So C=(D−W)/2 is half the difference of a convex piecewise-linear function of the tables and a sum of absolute values of linear functions. It is piecewise linear, and it has kinks.

A hidden edge is a coherent population (C=0) with an upward drift in one survey and the pattern weight turned up as far as the drift can hide. There the cut rule has no slack left, and sampling noise can push C^ either way. Everything in this chapter is a procedure aimed at that point.

16.2A toy with the same kink

Before the real problem, here is a small one that you can hold in your head and that we can simulate in a second. It is invented, and it is our own construction, not a research cycle. It keeps the three things that matter: a null that is a union of convex pieces, a statistic that is a difference of a convex function and an absolute value, and a Gaussian estimate. It drops everything else.

Let θ=(θ1,θ2) be a parameter in the plane, estimated by θ^ with independent coordinates, each with standard error 1/n. Write z=nθ^, so that z∼N(δ,I) with δ=nθ. The null is the union of two quadrants, H0: θ∈Q3∪Q1,Q3={θ1≤0,θ2≤0},Q1={θ1≥0,θ2≥0},H0: θ∈Q3∪Q1,Q3={θ1≤0,θ2≤0},Q1={θ1≥0,θ2≥0}, that is, the two coordinates do not have opposite signs. The statistic is φ(θ)=12(D(θ)−W(θ)),D=|θ1|+|θ2|,W=|θ1+θ2|.φ(θ)=12(D(θ)−W(θ)),D=|θ1|+|θ2|,W=|θ1+θ2|. Here D=maxλ∈{±1}2λ⋅θ is a value of a program over its dual vertices, which is the role D plays in the real problem, and W is an absolute value of a linear function. Work it out and φ(θ)=min(|θ1|,|θ2|) when the signs are opposite and 0 otherwise (Figure 16.1, left). It is non-negative, zero exactly on the null, and kinked along both axes. It is also the minimum of two pieces, φ=min(φ1,φ2),φ1=max(θ1,θ2,0),φ2=max(−θ1,−θ2,0),φ=min(φ1,φ2),φ1=max(θ1,θ2,0),φ2=max(−θ1,−θ2,0), where φ1 measures how far θ sits from the piece Q3 and φ2 how far from Q1. A point is in the null when one of the pieces is zero, which is the union.

Put the truth at the origin, the corner where all the kinks meet and the analogue of the hidden edge. Then z∼N(0,I), and the rule “reject when φ(z)>0” rejects exactly when the signs of z1 and z2 differ. That is half of all samples, 50 percent, at every sample size. The reason is Fang and Santos’s, and you can see it in the figure: nφ(θ^) does not converge to a Gaussian but to φ′(G), the directional derivative at the origin evaluated at the Gaussian limit, and φ′(h)=φ(h) is positive in two of the four quadrants of directions h. The toy is more violent than the real problem, where the same rule raised 14 to 21 percent. The mechanism is the same.

The three shaded regions of Figure 16.1 are the three repairs in miniature. At the origin there is a sharp test: reject when φ(z) exceeds the 95th percentile of φ(h) for h∼N(0,I), which solves 2{1−Φ(c)}2=0.05 and gives c=1.002. That is what a derivative bootstrap tries to reproduce from data, without being told that the truth is the origin. A union test cannot do that, because it asks each piece separately and rejects only when both pieces do: the piece Q3 is rejected beyond c1=1.955, the 95⁠th percentile of max(N1,N2,0), and so is Q1, and both together happen in the dark corners only, with probability 2{1−Φ(1.955)}2=0.13 percent. The rule is valid and nearly useless at this point. A bootstrap from a fitted null point sits in between, and I will come to where it can go wrong.

Figure 16.2 shows the same statistic as a landscape. The flat floor is the null, and the two ridges rise where neither piece can explain the point.

16.3Repair one: write the null as a union

The first repair says: if the null is a union of simple sets, test each simple set, and reject only when you have rejected all of them.

In the real problem, fix a direction for the crossings at every cut of every variable: this cut may be crossed upward but not downward, that one downward but not upward, and so on. Call the whole assignment a direction pattern s. With the pattern fixed, the tables have no shortfall exactly when they equal Asx for some x≥0, where x is a distribution over the joint outcomes of the six copies that cross only in the allowed directions, and As is the known matrix that maps such an x to the three tables. That is a vector equal to a known matrix times a non-negative vector, the null of Kitamura and Stoye (2018) and of Fang, Santos, Shaikh and Torgovitsky (2023). Any such x produces tables with C=0, because a one-directional crossing forces the margins to differ in that direction, and any tables with C=0 have a witness of this kind for some pattern. The cut-rule null is therefore the finite union of the sets {Asx:x≥0} over patterns s, exactly as the toy’s null is the union of Q1 and Q3.

The logic of the test is the intersection-union logic. Suppose the truth lies in the null, so that it lies in the set for some pattern s∗. The test that declares incoherence only when every admissible pattern is rejected rejects, whenever s∗ is admissible, only if the test for s∗ rejects, and that test has a level of its own. So the size of the union test is at most the size of the test for s∗, plus the probability that the step which chooses the admissible patterns drops s∗. That selection step is where the real work is. Experiment 18 fixes a cut’s direction from the sample when the two margins differ by more than log⁡n standard errors, and tries both directions otherwise, which leaves about 64 patterns in these designs. For each pattern it runs Kitamura and Stoye’s test: the squared distance from the sample to the cone {Asx:x≥0}, with the cone tightened by τ=log⁡n/n and a bootstrap recentered on the tightened estimate.

Two things are worth seeing in this construction. First, nothing new has to be proved about a non-differentiable function. Each pattern’s null is a cone, and a cone’s test is Kitamura and Stoye’s problem, so the validity of the whole test reduces to theirs plus the selection term. (We read their procedure and not their proof, and we have not checked that their conditions hold for every pattern here.) Second, a wrong choice of direction at a cut where the two margins are exactly equal still leaves a true pattern in the set. At such a cut the two crossing probabilities of any witness differ by the gap between the margins, which is zero, and the null requires one of them to be zero, so both are. The witness then lies in the set of both direction choices at that cut. That is not yet a bound on the size: which true pattern survives the selection then depends on the data, and the bound above holds one pattern fixed (the second exercise shows how much that can matter). The plainer size risk from too low a selection threshold sits at small but nonzero gaps, where it can drop every true pattern, the same thing that makes moment selection delicate. The toy has no selection step, because it has two pieces and tests both.

The price is power. At n=1000 with a drift present, many direction patterns fit the tables within sampling noise, and one pattern that is not rejected is enough to stop the test. In one incoherent sample, with C^=0.037, 24 of the 64 patterns were not rejected; their statistics ran from 0.13 to 0.57 against critical values from 0.40 to 0.99, and the patterns that were rejected were those forcing Z’s crossings downward at every cut. In the toy the same thing is plain: a union test needs both pieces to reject, and at a tie the pieces are rarely both far enough away.

16.4Repair two: bootstrap from the boundary

The second repair is the least theoretical, and I will explain how we got to it, because the story is the lesson. Cycle 15’s calibrated test resampled from a fitted null. You fit the closest tables that satisfy the null, resample n respondents per survey from the fit, and reject when the sample statistic exceeds the 95th percentile of the resampled statistics. To keep the fitted tables away from the edge of the cone, the fit gave every allowed joint outcome a minimum mass, the tightening that Kitamura and Stoye use. That test looked like a result. A look at its critical values showed them to be zero, so that it was the rule C^>0 again, and cycle 16’s stress test showed that resampling from a null pulled inward away from the boundary cannot see the boundary.

The diagnosis comes from Kitamura and Stoye’s own procedure. The bootstrap draws are moved onto the tightened restricted estimate, which they describe as recentered twice, once onto the null and a second time because the cone itself has been tightened; and the bootstrap statistic is then measured against the same tightened cone. Cycle 15 also centered its resamples on a tightened fit, but measured the shortfall against the untightened null; the error was that mismatch, not a missing recentering. The repair that worked was to drop the tightening altogether and resample from a fitted null point that sits on the boundary where the truth might be. That is the untightened null bootstrap.

It has no theorem. Nothing guarantees that a point fitted on the boundary shares the local geometry of the truth, which is what a derivative argument would need. The toy shows a small version of the worry. Fit the nearest point of Q1∪Q3 to each sample, resample around it, and reject when φ(z) exceeds the 95th percentile of the resampled values. At the corner the test is conservative, at 1.5 percent. Along the face θ=(0,−s) it climbs to 6.0 percent when the offset ns is between 2.5 and 3.5 standard errors and then settles near 5.5, which is what a 95th percentile read from 199 resamples gives even where the geometry is easy. The half point by which the middle exceeds that is small, but on the same simulated samples it is two to four Monte Carlo standard errors. A fitted point is only a good stand-in for the truth when the sample tells the two apart, and in the middle distance it cannot. That is a simulation of ours on a toy; what the real problem does is in the section after next.

16.5Repair three: bootstrap through the derivative

Fang and Santos (2019) give the general statement. If φ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at θ0 and the estimate has a Gaussian limit G, then n{φ(θ^)−φ(θ0)} converges to φθ0′(G). The standard bootstrap of φ is consistent if and only if φ is fully differentiable there, and a non-Gaussian limit signals failure. The repair is to bootstrap φ^n′(n(θ∗−θ^)), an estimate of the derivative composed with the usual bootstrap of the estimate, and to read the critical value from that. Generalized moment selection is a special case.

Our shortfall is such a function, and the memo’s reasoning is ours rather than theirs, since we did not check their formal conditions: D is a linear program value, hence convex and piecewise linear in the tables, W is a sum of absolute values, so C is piecewise linear. At a boundary point C=0 and C≥0 everywhere, so C′(h)≥0 in every direction, and nC^ converges to C′(G), which has an atom at zero and a positive tail. In experiment 17c (hidden edge, drift 0.1, 300 samples) the share of samples with nC^=0 stayed between 81.7 and 83.0 percent from n=1000 to 64,000, and the 95th percentile of nC^ stayed between 0.3 and 0.6 and did not shrink. That is the signature.

What has to be estimated is C′=(D′−W′)/2, and experiment 21 does it in two parts, each with its own tuning sequence. The derivative of D in a direction h is the largest value of λ⋅h over dual solutions λ within a slack δn=n−1/3 of optimal. The derivative of W takes the sign of the estimated gap at the cuts where it exceeds log⁡n standard errors and the absolute value elsewhere. The test rejects when nC^ exceeds the 95th percentile of the estimated derivative evaluated at n(p∗−p^). The toy has the same two parts, with D′ the maximum of λ⋅h over the four duals within a slack of the optimal value, and W′ the signed or absolute value of h1+h2 according to whether |z1+z2| exceeds log⁡n.

Figure 16.3 gives the toy at n=1000, with the slack n−1/3 in the same units (3.16 standard errors) and the sign threshold log⁡1000=2.63. Left: false alarms along the face θ=(0,−s), as a function of the offset d=ns in standard errors. Right: rejections along the alternative θ=(a,−a).

The picture has an uncomfortable shape. Far from the corner, at d=7, the face is smooth enough that every procedure that estimates the geometry correctly behaves: the null bootstrap and the derivative bootstrap are both at about 5.5 percent. At the corner, the derivative bootstrap with these tolerances is at 10 percent. The cause is a dropped dual vertex. For a sample in one opposite-sign quadrant, the vertex that belongs to the other one sits 2(|z1|+|z2|) below the optimum, more than the slack of 3.16 standard errors whenever min(|z1|,|z2|) is above about 0.8. Without it the estimated derivative is positive in the sample’s own quadrant only, the critical value falls from 1.00 to 0.76, and 2{1−Φ(0.76)}2 is 10 percent. In between, the two parts of the estimate can disagree about where the sample is: the sign threshold of 2.63 says “corner” while the dual slack says “face”, or both say “corner” when the truth is the face. Either way the critical value comes out below the face’s 1.645, and the test over-rejects. The sample has no local way to tell d=2.5 from d=0, since the threshold is about the size of the offset. This is the ordinary non-uniformity of pointwise theory. The toy exaggerates it, but it shows how a cell like the real problem’s hidden edge at drift 0.1 can carry an excess that depends on the tolerances, as that cell’s did. We did not test that mechanism in the real problem.

Loosening has a price too, and it is the same price everywhere. A larger slack admits more near-optimal duals, the maximum over a larger set can only rise, and the critical value rises with it. On the toy’s face, going from the slack n−1/3 to n−1/4 (5.62 standard errors) takes the false alarms at d=2.5 from 20.5 to 18.4 percent, and the power at a=2 from 78.6 to 75.6. Pushing the slack higher lowers the worst false alarm further, though in the toy never below about 15 percent, because the sign threshold’s misreadings remain, and the power falls with it (Figure 16.5, right).

16.6The price list

Put the evidence side by side (Figure 16.4). Each marker is one procedure in one cell of the real experiments. The cells are those in which the procedure was run; no procedure was run on all of them, and the sample counts differ (32 for the union test, 200 for the untightened bootstrap, 160 to 800 for the derivative bootstrap), so a difference of a percentage point or two carries no weight. With 200 samples, a true rate of 2.5 percent has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 1.1 points.

The ranking is clear in the lower panel and uncomfortable in the upper. The rule C^>0 has the most power and fails the level, which makes its power uninformative. Of the other three, the union test is the least powerful by a wide margin at n=1000 (6 percent against 54 and 63.5) and catches up at n=4000 (88, 99 and 100). The derivative bootstrap has the most power of the three, but it is the only one of the three with a null cell above nominal, and its comparison with the others is not size-adjusted.

Union test Untightened bootstrap Derivative bootstrap
What stands behind it Validity reduces to Kitamura and Stoye per pattern, plus the selection step Simulation only; no theorem Fang and Santos’s theorem, conditions not checked here
Worst null cell 0 of 32 in each cell tried 2.5 percent, across 24 cells 7.1 percent of 800, one cell
Power under drift, n=1000 / 4000 6 / 88 percent 54 / 99 percent 63.5 / 100 percent
Tuning you must choose Selection threshold for directions, and the tightening τ None, beyond the null point fitted Dual slack, and sign threshold

16.7What the papers say

What the paper says: Fang and Santos (2019), Inference on directionally differentiable functions

This is the source of the diagnosis and of the third repair. We read the abstract and Sections 3.2 and 3.3, which contain the statement that for a Hadamard directionally differentiable function of an estimator with a Gaussian limit the standard bootstrap is consistent exactly when the function is fully differentiable (their Theorem 3.1), the corollary that a non-Gaussian limit signals failure, and the construction that composes an estimate of the derivative with the bootstrap (their Theorem 3.2). We did not read the rest. The sections we read do not say how to choose the sequence that governs the derivative estimate; their rate conditions allow more than one choice, which is why the slack in experiment 21 is a free parameter here. That the shortfall is such a function, and that its derivative is estimated as we describe, is our application of their theory; we did not check their conditions for this program, and the estimated derivative takes negative values in some directions where the true one cannot, which is harmless for the upper quantile and a sign that the estimate is rough.

What the paper says: Fang, Santos, Shaikh and Torgovitsky (2023), Inference for large-scale linear systems with known coefficients

They test whether a vector β(P) equals Ax for some x≥0, with A a known matrix. We read the abstract, the introduction, the statement of their Theorem 3.1 and Remarks 3.1 and 3.2, and, later, Section 4.1 where the test statistic is defined. The theorem says such an x exists exactly when β is in the range of A and a sign condition holds for the minimum-norm solution. The test is built on this and is meant for a large number of columns, where eliminating the unknowns one at a time, to rewrite the null as inequalities, is infeasible. Their statistic is the larger of two linear programs, one that detects β outside the range of A and one that detects a sign violation. In the pooled survey problem of Chapters 8 and 10 we read these as the margin and loop parts of the split of the Kitamura and Stoye statistic, which is our observation and not theirs. We did not read the critical value (Section 4.3) or the proofs, and we have not run their test on anything. It is the candidate for the next step, below.

What the paper says: Kitamura and Stoye (2018), Nonparametric analysis of random utility models

Chapters 8 and 10 cover the test. What matters here is its handling of the boundary: shrink the cone by τN with NτN→∞, move the bootstrap draws onto the shrunken estimate, and measure the bootstrap statistic against the shrunken cone. We read the abstract and Sections 1 to 3.2 and 4.1 to 4.3 of the arXiv version, and re-read Section 4.2 for the double recentering; we did not read the rest, including the application, the Monte Carlo and the appendices. We had first quoted a sentence of theirs about the second recentering, and a check against the stored text did not find the sentence as we wrote it, so the book paraphrases. Whether their proof covers contexts whose margins are shared and differ is something we did not check.

What the paper says: Hong and Li (2018), The numerical delta method

This is the numerical-derivative alternative to Fang and Santos, and we could not obtain it: SSRN and the publisher’s page both blocked the request, and we have metadata only. Nothing in this chapter depends on what it says, and we cannot say whether its step-size conditions would settle the slack question.

16.8What we found

Cycle 16 and the baseline. The stress test put populations on the boundary between C=0 and C>0, found by bisection, and counted how often C^>0. False alarms in percent, rule C^>0, 400 samples per cell (experiment 16, and experiment 17b for the last two columns, 300 samples):

n per survey 200 1000 4000 16000 64000
Threshold, equal margins 5.3 4.8 5.5 6.7 4.7
Hidden edge, drift 0.1 7.5 13.8 18.8 17.0 21.0
Hidden edge, drift 0.4 24.3 16.5 19.3 14.7 16.3

At the hidden edge the rule raises false alarms at 1.5 to 5 times the nominal level, and 2 to 4 times from n=1000 on. Random populations on the boundary fail more mildly on average and badly in their worst cases (34 percent for the worst of 40 populations, a maximum inflated by selection). Experiment 17d checked that these rates are not solver artifacts: with 300 samples per cell at n=4000, raising the threshold for “positive” from 10−9 to 10−6 or 10−5 changed none of them (3.3, 19.0 and 17.7 percent).

The first repair that failed, and the one that worked. Cycle 15’s tightened bootstrap raised at most 4.5 percent false alarms in its cells and detected 97 percent of incoherent systems at the largest drift at n=1000, against 61 percent for cycle 13’s rule. That looked like a result. The check that undid it was a look at the critical values: the 95th percentile of the null distribution was zero in every sample inspected. In experiment 16b, 200 samples with 100 resamples each:

Declares incoherent, percent Tightened Untightened
Hidden edge, drift 0.2, n=1000 (null) 19.0 2.5
Hidden edge, drift 0.4, n=200 (null) 18.5 1.5
Incoherent, drift 0.4, n=1000 (power) 97.5 55.0

Without tightening the critical value was positive in 71.5 to 99.5 percent of samples, the level was restored in both hidden-edge cells, and the power fell to about where cycle 13’s rule had it. The earlier gain in power had been bought with false alarms.

The union test (experiment 18, with 18b and 18c). Thirty-two samples per cell, 60 resamples, about 64 patterns, the selection threshold log⁡n standard errors:

Declares incoherent Union test C^>0
Hidden edge, drift 0.4, n=1000 (null) 0 of 32 3 of 32
Hidden edge, drift 0.4, n=4000 (null) 0 of 32 6 of 32
Incoherent, drift 0.4, n=1000 (power) 2 of 32 30 of 32
Incoherent, drift 0.4, n=4000 (power) 28 of 32 32 of 32
Pattern weight 0.7, drift 0.4, n=1000 (power) 32 of 32 32 of 32

The last two rows are experiment 18b. Thirty-two samples bound the size only loosely: zero of 32 has a one-sided 95 percent upper limit of about 9 percent. The memo had first said the union test had “almost no power”; the last two rows corrected that to what it is, low power for a moderate contradiction with drift at n=1000 that rises quickly with the sample size and with the strength of the contradiction.

Experiment 18c tested the selection step directly, at n=1000. Trying only the sample’s own direction pattern (threshold κ=0, about one pattern per sample) the two null cells, hidden edge with drift 0.05 and with drift 0.4, again gave 0 of 32, and power rose from 2 to 5 of 32. A higher threshold of one standard error (130 patterns on average in the drift 0.05 cell and 27 in the drift 0.4 cell) also gave 0 of 32 in both null cells. The tie argument above is a proof that a true pattern survives an exact tie. The 0 of 32 is empirical, from 32 samples in one design, and does not show that small nonzero gaps are harmless in general. Most of the distance between the union test’s 2 or 5 of 32 and the invalid rule’s 30 lies in Kitamura and Stoye’s statistic, a squared distance between cell probabilities, and not in the union over patterns.

The untightened bootstrap across all boundary designs (experiment 17). The designs were those of cycle 16 plus incoherent systems, with 200 samples and 100 resamples per cell. False alarms of the bootstrap, in percent, with the rule on the same samples:

With one survey of 300 and two of 4,000 the bootstrap gave 0, 0 and 1 percent (the rule 9.5, 7.5 and 6), and on six random boundary populations at n=1000 it gave 0 to 0.5 percent (the rule 1.5 to 15). In all 24 null cells it never exceeded 2.5 percent. Its power, with the rule’s on the same samples, was 98.5 percent (rule 100) with pattern weight 0.5 and no drift at n=1000; 54 (95) and 99 (100) with drift 0.4 at n=1000 and 4000; and in the weak case, pattern weight 0.36 and C=0.02, 6 (34.5) and 23 (78). It is conservative everywhere we tried it. That is evidence about these 24 cells and about nothing else.

At n=1000 it held the level in the three null cells and had more power than the two other procedures that did: 63.5 percent with drift against 54 for the untightened bootstrap and 6 for the union test, and 18 percent in the weak case against 6. At n=4000 its power rose to 100 and 52.5 percent, and one null cell, the hidden edge with drift 0.1, gave 7.5 percent, 12 of 160. That is 1.5 Monte Carlo standard errors from 5 percent, not enough to decide, so we reran the cell with 640 fresh samples and got 7.0 percent; pooled, 57 of 800, or 7.1 percent, about 2.8 standard errors above 5 percent. The excess is modest and real.

The tuning check. The over-rejection looked like a tuning effect, and the way to find out was a paired comparison. On the same 320 samples and bootstrap draws of that cell, with only the dual slack changed, the slack n−1/3 gave 24 false alarms in 320 (7.5 percent, median critical value 0.33), and n−1/4 gave 4 in 320 (1.25 percent, median critical value 0.78). Because the critical values can only rise with the slack, 20 of the 24 rejections simply disappear. On the same 200 samples of the power cell at n=1000 (weight 0.5, drift 0.4), the same change cut the power from 66 to 38 percent, with the median critical value rising from 0.92 to 1.45. The run behind the table used 150 resamples and gave 63.5 percent; the paired run drew 200 fresh samples (its seeds differ from the table’s, and the rule C^>0 gives 96 rather than 95.5 percent on them) and used 120 resamples, and its 66 percent is about half a Monte Carlo standard error from 63.5.

Mistakes along the way. These are set out here, because each one changed a claim. The tightened bootstrap’s 97 percent power was bought with false alarms (above). The first draft of the union test’s description said it had almost no power; experiment 18b corrected it. Experiment 18’s random seed was first built from Python’s string hash, which differs from one process to the next, and we replaced it before the run. An independent review of cycle 17 then corrected the memo’s summary, which had said that three procedures “held the level” without stating that the derivative bootstrap’s 7.5 percent cell was an exception; replaced “valid by construction” with “validity reduces to Kitamura and Stoye’s”, plus the selection term; and restricted the claim that sampling noise biases the shortfall downward, and so makes the rule conservative, to populations whose margins are equal or nearly equal. At the hidden edge C^>0 in up to 26 percent of null samples across cycles 16 and 17. It also corrected the cycle 16 statement that the rule fails at three to five times the nominal level to 1.5 to 5 times. The review confirmed the identity D=W+2C, the piecewise linearity of C and C′≥0 on the boundary, and the large-n evidence that P(C^>0) does not shrink; its own direct computation of P(C′(G)>0) gives about 6 percent at the threshold and 19 percent at both hidden edges, which fits the simulated rates.

The next candidate. The test of Fang, Santos, Shaikh and Torgovitsky is the obvious replacement for Kitamura and Stoye’s statistic inside the union test, since the memo’s guess is that the statistic, not the union, is where the union test loses most of its power. The other open step is a rule for the derivative bootstrap’s dual slack, one that does not simply trade one error for the other. We have done neither.

Try it

Try it 16.1. In the toy, show that 12(D−W)=min(|θ1|,|θ2|) when the signs of the two coordinates differ and 0 otherwise. Then compute the rule φ>0’s false-alarm rate with the truth at the origin, and solve 2{1−Φ(c)}2=0.05 for the critical value of a test that is exact there. You should get one half, and c≈1.00.

Try it 16.2. A data-dependent set S of patterns is chosen, and the union test rejects only when every pattern in S is rejected. Each pattern’s test has level α when the truth lies in that pattern’s null, and is computed from the data whether or not the pattern is in S. Fix one true pattern s∗ and show that the probability of a false alarm is at most α plus the probability that S leaves out s∗. Where does the data-dependence of S enter, and why is it harmless for the first term? Then find two true patterns and a rule for S that always keeps one of them, under which the false-alarm probability is close to 2α.

Try it 16.3. At a cut where the two margins have equal distribution functions, the two crossing probabilities of any coupling differ by F1(l)−F2(l) and the null requires the smaller of them to be zero. Show that this forces both to be zero, and say what that implies for a wrong direction choice at an exact tie, and why it does not extend to a small nonzero gap.

Try it 16.4. For the toy at n=1000 the sign threshold is log⁡n=2.63. By looking at the distribution of z1+z2 at θ=(0,−s), find the offsets d=ns at which you expect the threshold to misclassify the face as a tie about as often as it classifies it correctly, and compare your answer with the worst offset in Figure 16.3.

Try it 16.5. In Figure 16.3, set n=1000 and the truth to (0,−0.08), an offset of about 2.5 standard errors, and read the four rates. Switch the dual slack from n−1/3 to n−1/4 and watch the derivative bootstrap’s false alarms and then its power at (0.06,−0.06). Then run the sweep along the face and compare where each procedure’s false alarms peak and how high they get. Set up Figure 16.3 · Switch the slack to n−1/4
